On 10/13/07, chromatic  wrote:
> On Friday 12 October 2007 19:10:55 A. Pagaltzis wrote:
> > * chromatic  [2007-10-13 00:05]:
>
> > > On Friday 12 October 2007 13:36:50 A. Pagaltzis wrote:
>
> > >> I hate to bring it up, and I'm not particularly fond of
> > >> dumping on Perl6, but compare how that effort is going with
> > >> the Python 3000 track record, which took the "internal
> > >> refactoring and juggling (and it's OK to break backcompat)"
> > >> approach vs. the "complete retink" approach of Perl6.
>
> > > Clearly the problem is that Perl 6 has no Daddy Googlebucks
> > > funding 20 - 50% of development time.
>
> > Sorry? A single partially-funded developer working for about a
> > year is capable of delivering more than all of the volunteer work
> > that has gone into Pugs and its multiple backends over several
> > years? That's bogus.
> >
> > I think it's rather clearly the problem that with Resources and
> > Quality being fixed in place and Time being a free variable, the
> > Scope knob is the only one you can turn; and that was obviously
> > dialed down a lot on the Py3k project to keep the Time variable
> > from exploding.
>
> My point was that Python 3000's Resources knob has settings higher than 1.5,
> which is sadly where the Perl 6 and Perl 5 knobs have been stuck, combined,
> for several years now.
>
> If I count correctly, the only person actually spending any day-job time
> working on Perl 5 or 6 with any official blessing from an employer is Jan.
> Maybe Rafael.

Then you missed the year I worked fulltime on perl. Or am I not
included because my employer was me? Admittedly once I started working
on a new job, writing a book, and moving house my contributions
dropped to zero, but thats life.

And to comment on this thread, im with Aristotle here. There seems to
be a tendency in Perl circles to take the position that there are only
two possibilities, a) work on Perl6, a totally new language, or b)
maintain Perl 5 with 0 tolerance for backcompat breakage.

I think there is a middle ground. Try to keep as much of Perl5 as
possible but focus on cleaning up the internals and if a few things of
Perl5 must be sacrificed to achieve this then so be it. And I include
the XS code out there in the "few things".

This isnt a binary scenario people, its not just a choice of Perll5
versus Perl6, there are other options. And I think Kurila does belong
on list for the time being as it proves that there is another choice.
Having said that Im not super keen on Kurila as I dont think its aimed
at the problems that I think hold Perl5 back. But its mere existence
proves that there are more options than are conventionally postulated.
And I think that reminder is important to this community. Personally i
think that if we can start thinking outside of the box a bit we might
realize that there is a perfectly viable future for perl5 that doesn't
involve being slavishly devoted to backwards compatibility and that
isn't called Perl6.

Yves
